project-brief
How to write a project brief that gets useful answers
Product planning
Start with the situation, not a feature list

A useful brief explains what is happening today and what should become easier. Instead of asking for an app with login, chat and payments, describe who will use it and the problem they need to solve. A local shop, for example, might need customers to see available products and request delivery without repeated phone calls. That context helps a development partner suggest an appropriate first release.
Describe one complete user journey

Walk through the most important task from beginning to end. Who starts it? What information do they provide? Who reviews it? What counts as completion? For a booking product, this might mean choosing a service, checking availability, confirming a time and receiving a reminder. Include the staff side too: someone may need to manage cancellations or correct a booking. A short, concrete example often reveals more than a long list of screen names.
Separate requirements from preferences

Mark each item as essential for launch, useful later or still open for discussion. Mention constraints such as an existing database, a particular payment provider or a deadline tied to an event. Share design references, but explain what you like about them: their navigation, visual style or checkout flow. This gives the designer direction without assuming the entire reference product needs to be reproduced.
Make room for practical questions

State a budget range if one is available, the people who will approve decisions and what materials already exist. Useful materials include branding files, sample content, API documentation and access to a current product. Ask for an estimate with assumptions and exclusions, rather than expecting an exact price from an early paragraph. The next step should be a shared understanding of scope, risks and what needs clarification before work begins.
launch-handover
What a useful software project handover should include
Project delivery
Treat handover as part of the delivery

A product can be ready for users while its owner still lacks the information needed to operate it. Agree on handover deliverables during project planning and review them before the final release. The aim is simple: the people responsible for the product should understand where it runs, how changes are released and who can help when something stops working. The exact documents should match the complexity of the product.
Know which accounts belong to the business

Create a clear inventory of source repositories, hosting services, domains, databases, app store accounts and external integrations. Record the owner and purpose of each account, together with any recurring costs. Share access through the service’s supported invitation or role system where possible. A handover document should point to the appropriate account or secret-management process rather than contain passwords or private API keys.
Document the everyday operating tasks

Focus documentation on actions someone will actually need to take. Explain how to publish an update, change content, inspect a reported error and contact the right provider. Include the setup steps required to work with the source code and note dependencies on external systems. If backup and recovery are in scope, document the agreed process and how it has been checked. A short, accurate operating guide is more useful than a large document nobody can follow.
Agree what happens after release

Keep a visible list of accepted limitations, remaining work and proposed improvements. Clarify how a newly reported issue will be assessed, which support hours are included and how additional development is approved. A walkthrough with the product owner can reveal missing access or unclear instructions while the delivery team is still available. Completing that walkthrough gives both sides a practical point of reference for the next phase.
maintenance-planning
Planning maintenance before your app goes live
Product operations
Give the live product an owner

Launching an application is the beginning of operating it. Someone needs to review user reports, make product decisions and coordinate technical work. That person does not need to fix every issue, but they should know how a problem is reported and who is responsible for the next action. Establishing ownership early makes support more predictable for both the business and the development team.
Separate urgent problems from improvements

A sign-in failure affecting users needs a different response from a request for a new dashboard filter. Define a small set of issue priorities based on user impact and agree how they are communicated. Keep improvements in a separate backlog so that they can be planned deliberately. Include useful details in reports: the action attempted, the result, the device or environment and steps that reproduce the problem. Avoid collecting unnecessary personal information in screenshots or logs.
Budget for the services behind the app

Hosting, databases, messaging, maps, AI services and other integrations may have ongoing costs. Record which services are used and who monitors their usage. Review whether a change in customer activity could change those costs. Maintenance discussions should also cover access ownership, dependency updates and release preparation. The right level of support depends on the application and the consequences of downtime; one standard package will not fit every product.
Keep a manageable improvement cycle

Collect feedback and review it on an agreed schedule. Group related issues, identify the journeys causing the most friction and choose a small set of improvements for the next release. Check the affected user journeys before shipping and keep release notes that explain meaningful changes. Consistent, focused improvements help a product remain understandable to its users and maintainable for the people building it.
